title: Independence, Basis and Dimension
summary: A subspace such as a plane in $\R^3$ contains infinitely many vectors, yet two well-chosen vectors describe all of it. This chapter makes that precise. We call a list of vectors independent when none is redundant, a basis when it is independent and spans,…

intro.x: A subspace such as a plane in $\R^3$ contains infinitely many vectors, yet two well-chosen vectors describe all of it. This chapter makes that precise. We call a list of vectors independent when none is redundant, a basis when it is independent and spans, and we prove the fundamental fact that every basis of a space has the same number of vectors: the dimension. Dimension is the one number that classifies finite-dimensional vector spaces.

blocks.x: Vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ in a vector space $V$ are linearly independent if the only solution of
c_1\mathbf{v}_1+\dots+c_k\mathbf{v}_k=\mathbf{0}
is $c_1=\dots=c_k=0$. They are linearly dependent if some nontrivial choice of scalars gives $\mathbf{0}$.
Vectors $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ are dependent if and only if at least one of them is a linear combination of the others. In that case removing it does not change the span.

If $\sum c_i\mathbf{v}_i=\mathbf{0}$ with some $c_j
e0$, solve for $\mathbf{v}_j=-\sum_{i
e j}(c_i/c_j)\mathbf{v}_i$. Conversely, if $\mathbf{v}_j=\sum_{i
e j}a_i\mathbf{v}_i$ then $\mathbf{v}_j-\sum a_i\mathbf{v}_i=\mathbf{0}$ is a nontrivial relation. Any combination using $\mathbf{v}_j$ can be rewritten without it, so the span is unchanged.
Testing independence in $\R^m$
Put the vectors as columns of $A=[\mathbf{v}_1\cdots\mathbf{v}_k]$. The relation $\sum c_i\mathbf{v}_i=\mathbf{0}$ is $A\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}$. Hence:
The columns of $A$ are independent iff $\Null A=\{\mathbf{0}\}$, iff $A$ has a pivot in every column (no free variables). In particular any $k>m$ vectors in $\R^m$ are dependent.
Are $(1,2,1)$, $(2,1,0)$, $(4,5,2)$ independent? Row reduce $\begin{pmatrix}1&2&4\\2&1&5\\1&0&2\end{pmatrix}$:
\to\begin{pmatrix}1&2&4\\0&-3&-3\\0&-2&-2\end{pmatrix}\to\begin{pmatrix}1&2&4\\0&1&1\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
The third column is not a pivot column, so the vectors are dependent; indeed $(4,5,2)=2(1,2,1)+(2,1,0)$.

The functions $1,t,t^2$ are independent in $C[0,1]$: if $c_0+c_1t+c_2t^2=0$ for all $t$, a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $2$ would have infinitely many roots. By contrast $\sin^2t$, $\cos^2t$ and $1$ are dependent, since $\sin^2t+\cos^2t-1=0$.
A list containing $\mathbf{0}$ is dependent; a single vector $\mathbf{v}$ is independent iff $\mathbf{v}\neq\mathbf{0}$.
Any sublist of an independent list is independent.
If $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ are independent and $\mathbf{w}\notin\Span\{\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k\}$, then $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k,\mathbf{w}$ are independent.
Nonzero eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent (Chapter 13); pairwise orthogonal nonzero vectors are independent (Chapter 1, Exercise 1.8).

(i) $1\cdot\mathbf{0}=\mathbf{0}$ is a nontrivial relation; for a single nonzero vector $c\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$ forces $c=0$. (ii) A relation among the sublist is a relation among the full list with zeros elsewhere. (iii) If $\sum c_i\mathbf{v}_i+d\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}$ with $d\ne0$ then $\mathbf{w}\in\Span\{\mathbf{v}_i\}$, a contradiction; so $d=0$ and then all $c_i=0$ by independence.
A list $\mathcal{B}=(\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_n)$ is a basis of $V$ if it is linearly independent and spans $V$.
The key property of a basis is unique coordinates.

$(\mathbf{b}_1,\dots,\mathbf{b}_n)$ is a basis of $V$ if and only if every $\mathbf{v}\in V$ can be written in exactly one way as $\mathbf{v}=x_1\mathbf{b}_1+\dots+x_n\mathbf{b}_n$. The scalars $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ are the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis, written $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}\in\R^n$.

Existence of the representation is exactly “spans”. If $\sum x_i\mathbf{b}_i=\sum y_i\mathbf{b}_i$ then $\sum(x_i-y_i)\mathbf{b}_i=\mathbf{0}$, so $x_i=y_i$ for all $i$ if and only if the list is independent.

$\mathbf{e}_1,\dots,\mathbf{e}_n$ is the standard basis of $\R^n$; $1,t,\dots,t^n$ is a basis of $\mathcal{P}_n$, so $\mathcal{P}_n$ has $n+1$ coordinates; the matrices $E_{ij}$ with a single $1$ in position $(i,j)$ form a basis of $\R^{m\times n}$, which has $mn$ elements.

In $\R^2$, $\mathcal{B}=((1,1),(1,-1))$ is a basis, because the matrix with these columns has determinant $-2\ne0$. To find the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}=(5,1)$, solve $x_1(1,1)+x_2(1,-1)=(5,1)$: $x_1+x_2=5$, $x_1-x_2=1$, so $[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}=(3,2)$.
$n$ vectors in $\R^n$ form a basis iff the square matrix having them as columns is invertible, iff its determinant is nonzero.

By Theorem 3.12 the columns are independent iff $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has only the zero solution iff $A$ is invertible, and then $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is solvable for all $\mathbf{b}$, so the columns also span.
How many vectors can a basis have? The following lemma is the engine of the whole theory.
If $V$ is spanned by $m$ vectors, then any independent list in $V$ has at most $m$ vectors.

Let $\mathbf{w}_1,\dots,\mathbf{w}_m$ span $V$ and let $\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_k$ be independent; suppose $k>m$. Write each $\mathbf{u}_j=\sum_{i=1}^ma_{ij}\mathbf{w}_i$. The $m\times k$ system $A\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{0}$ with $A=(a_{ij})$ has more unknowns than equations, so it has a nontrivial solution $\mathbf{c}$ (Corollary 2.13). Then
\sum_jc_j\mathbf{u}_j=\sum_i\Big(\sum_ja_{ij}c_j\Big)\mathbf{w}_i=\mathbf{0}
is a nontrivial relation, contradicting independence.
If $V$ has a finite basis, then every basis of $V$ has the same number of elements. This number is the dimension $\dim V$.
Let $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ be bases with $n$ and $m$ elements. $\mathcal{B}$ is independent and $\mathcal{C}$ spans, so $n\le m$ by the lemma. Exchanging the roles gives $m\le n$.
By convention $\dim\{\mathbf{0}\}=0$ (the empty list is its basis). A space with no finite spanning list is infinite-dimensional ($\mathcal{P}$, $C[a,b]$, $\R^\infty$).
$\dim\R^n=n$; $\dim\mathcal{P}_n=n+1$; $\dim\R^{m\times n}=mn$; the space of symmetric $n\times n$ matrices has dimension $\tfrac12n(n+1)$; the solution space of $y''-3y'+2y=0$ has dimension $2$.
Let $\dim V=n$. Then
every independent list has at most $n$ vectors, and every spanning list at least $n$;
any $n$ independent vectors form a basis;
any $n$ spanning vectors form a basis;
every independent list can be extended to a basis, and every spanning list contains a basis.

(i) is the exchange lemma applied to a basis. For (iv), extend an independent list by adding vectors outside its span one at a time (Theorem 7.6(iii)); the process stops after at most $n$ steps, when the span is all of $V$. To shrink a spanning list, delete any vector that is a combination of the others (Proposition 7.2) until the list is independent. For (ii): extend the $n$ independent vectors to a basis; a basis has $n$ elements, so nothing was added. For (iii): shrink to a basis; it has $n$ elements, so nothing was removed.

To prove that $n$ given vectors form a basis of an $n$-dimensional space, you need only check one of independence or spanning, not both. In $\R^n$, checking $\det\ne0$ is the quickest. This halves the work in many proofs and exam problems.
If $W$ is a subspace of a finite-dimensional $V$, then $\dim W\le\dim V$, with equality if and only if $W=V$.

A basis of $W$ is an independent list in $V$, so has at most $\dim V$ vectors. If $\dim W=\dim V=n$, a basis of $W$ is $n$ independent vectors in $V$, hence a basis of $V$ by the counting theorem, so $W=V$.
Consequently the subspaces of $\R^3$ are $\{\mathbf{0}\}$ (dimension $0$), lines through $\mathbf{0}$ (dimension $1$), planes through $\mathbf{0}$ (dimension $2$) and $\R^3$, as claimed in Chapter 6.
For subspaces $U,W$ of a finite-dimensional space,
\dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W).

Take a basis $\mathbf{c}_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}_r$ of $U\cap W$ and extend it to a basis $\mathbf{c}_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}_r,\mathbf{u}_1,\dots,\mathbf{u}_s$ of $U$ and a basis $\mathbf{c}_1,\dots,\mathbf{c}_r,\mathbf{w}_1,\dots,\mathbf{w}_t$ of $W$. Then the $r+s+t$ vectors $\mathbf{c}_i,\mathbf{u}_j,\mathbf{w}_k$ span $U+W$. They are independent: if $\sum a_i\mathbf{c}_i+\sum b_j\mathbf{u}_j+\sum d_k\mathbf{w}_k=\mathbf{0}$ then $\sum d_k\mathbf{w}_k=-\sum a_i\mathbf{c}_i-\sum b_j\mathbf{u}_j\in U\cap W$, so it is a combination of the $\mathbf{c}_i$, and independence of the basis of $W$ forces all $d_k=0$; then independence of the basis of $U$ gives $a_i=b_j=0$. So $\dim(U+W)=r+s+t=(r+s)+(r+t)-r$.
Two distinct planes $U,W$ through the origin in $\R^3$ satisfy $\dim(U+W)=3$ and $\dim U+\dim W=4$, so $\dim(U\cap W)=1$: they meet in a line.

sections.title: Coordinates make every space look like $\R^n$

blocks.x: If $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of an $n$-dimensional space $V$, the map $\mathbf{v}\mapsto[\mathbf{v}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ is a bijection $V\to\R^n$ that preserves sums and scalar multiples. Every question about $V$ (independence, span, dimension) can therefore be translated into a question about columns of numbers, answerable by elimination. This is why the abstract theory is no harder in practice than the concrete one.

In $\mathcal{P}_2$ with basis $(1,t,t^2)$, the polynomials $p_1=1+t$, $p_2=t+t^2$, $p_3=1-t^2$ have coordinate vectors $(1,1,0)$, $(0,1,1)$, $(1,0,-1)$. Row reduction of these columns gives $\det=\begin{vmatrix}1&0&1\\1&1&0\\0&1&-1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot(-1)-0+1\cdot1=0$, so $p_1,p_2,p_3$ are dependent: indeed $p_1-p_2=1-t^2=p_3$.

blocks.name: Common pitfall
blocks.title: coordinates depend on the basis and its order

blocks.x: The vector $(3,2)$ in the previous example is not the point $(5,1)$; it is the recipe “$3$ copies of $(1,1)$ and $2$ of $(1,-1)$”. Changing the basis or even reordering it changes the coordinate vector. Chapter 10 studies exactly how coordinates transform.
Vectors are independent when the only relation among them is the trivial one; dependence means one is redundant.
A basis is an independent spanning list; it gives each vector a unique coordinate vector.
The exchange lemma shows all bases have the same size, the dimension.
In dimension $n$: any $n$ independent or any $n$ spanning vectors form a basis; independent lists extend, spanning lists shrink to bases.
$\dim(U+W)=\dim U+\dim W-\dim(U\cap W)$.
Coordinates identify every $n$-dimensional space with $\R^n$.
Decide whether $(1,0,1,2)$, $(0,1,1,1)$, $(2,1,3,5)$ are independent, and find a basis of their span.
Show that $(1,1,0)$, $(0,1,1)$, $(1,0,1)$ is a basis of $\R^3$ and find the coordinates of $(2,3,5)$.
Prove that $\sin t$, $\cos t$, $\sin 2t$ are independent in $C[0,2\pi]$. (Hint: evaluate at several points, or integrate against each.)
Let $V$ be a $5$-dimensional space and $U,W$ subspaces of dimensions $3$ and $4$. What are the possible values of $\dim(U\cap W)$?
Find a basis and the dimension of $\{A\in\R^{3\times3}: A\T=-A\}$ (skew-symmetric) and of $\{A\in\R^{3\times3}:\tr A=0\}$.
Prove that if $\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_k$ are independent and $A$ is an invertible $n\times n$ matrix then $A\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,A\mathbf{v}_k$ are independent. Is the invertibility needed?
Show that $\dim\R^\infty=\infty$ by exhibiting, for each $n$, $n$ independent sequences.
